section.title: Peter's Confession
section.sectionRationale: This is the hinge of the Gospel. At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, and Jesus begins to reveal that the Christ must suffer, die, and rise. To follow this Messiah is to take up a cross.
section.thesis: Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, confessed by revelation and destined to build His church; yet He is a crucified Messiah, and those who would follow Him must deny themselves, take up their cross, and lose their lives to find them.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the confession at Caesarea Philippi and the promise to build the church; the first passion prediction and Peter's rebuke; and the call to take up the cross and follow.

verses.text: When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, He questioned His disciples: “Who do people say the Son of Man is?”
They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.”
“But what about you?” Jesus asked. “Who do you say I am?”
Simon Peter answered, “You are the {{christos|Christ}}, the Son of the living God.”
Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For this was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by My Father in heaven.
And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this {{petra|rock}} I will build My {{ekklesia|church}}, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”
Then He admonished the disciples not to tell anyone that He was the Christ.

From that time on Jesus began to show His disciples that He must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things at the hands of the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.
Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him. “Far be it from You, Lord!” he said. “This shall never happen to You!”
But Jesus turned and said to Peter, “Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me. For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.”

units.label: Take up your cross
units.note: lose your life to find it

verses.text: Then Jesus told His disciples, “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.
For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.
What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world, yet forfeits his {{psyche|soul}}? Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul?
For the Son of Man will come in His Father’s glory with His angels, and then He will repay each one according to what he has done.
Truly I tell you, some who are standing here will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom.”

christos.gloss: The Anointed One, the Messiah, God's promised King. Peter's confession names Jesus not merely a prophet but the Christ, the Son of the living God, the one all Scripture anticipates.

petra.gloss: A rock or bedrock, a massive foundation stone, distinct from petros, a stone or boulder, which is Peter's name. The wordplay links Peter, the confessing apostle, to the rock on which Christ builds, the confessed truth that Jesus is the Christ.

ekklesia.gloss: An assembly, the gathered people, the church. Jesus calls it My church, His own new-covenant community, which He Himself will build and which death itself cannot overpower.

psyche.gloss: Life or soul, the whole self that lives. To lose one's psyche for Christ is to find it; to gain the world at its cost is the ruin of everything, for no price can buy it back.

basic.context: At Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks His disciples who people say He is, then who they say He is. Peter answers, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus blesses him, promises to build His church, and gives the keys of the kingdom. Then He begins to teach that the Christ must suffer, die, and rise. Peter rebukes Him and is sharply corrected. Following this Messiah, Jesus says, means denying yourself and taking up your cross.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the turning point of the Gospel: the identity of Jesus is settled, and from here the road runs to the cross. The confession is right, but Peter's idea of the Christ is wrong, which is why Jesus at once redefines messiahship as suffering. Note the debated meaning of the rock and the keys, and the puzzling promise that some will see the Son of Man coming before they die.
basic.originalLanguages: Peter confesses Jesus as the Christos, the anointed King. Jesus plays on names: Peter, petros, a stone, and the petra, the bedrock, on which He builds His ekklesia, His church. And He warns that gaining the world while forfeiting the psyche, the soul or life, is total loss.
basic.typology: Jesus building His church on the rock echoes God as the Rock of Israel and the temple built on a foundation stone. The suffering and rising Christ fulfills the pattern of the righteous sufferer and the servant of Isaiah 53.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and He is the crucified and risen Christ. He builds an indestructible church, holds the keys of the kingdom, and calls His people to follow Him in the way of the cross before He comes in glory.
basic.god: The Father reveals the Son to Peter; saving knowledge is God's gift, not human insight. God's way of victory runs through suffering, overturning human expectations, and He will finally repay each person according to what they have done.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53 foretells the suffering servant. Psalm 118 speaks of the rejected stone become the cornerstone. Matthew 18 repeats the binding and loosing to the church. Romans 1 confesses Jesus as Son of God in power by the resurrection.
basic.oneStory: The Gospel turns here: Jesus is confessed as the Christ, and the Christ is revealed as one who must die and rise. The church is founded on this confession, and the way of discipleship is the way of the cross. The whole story now bends toward Jerusalem, where the Son of the living God will lay down His life and rise, building a church the gates of death cannot overcome.

context.literary:
The passage is the hinge of Matthew's Gospel. Verse 21 opens with 'From that time on Jesus began', a phrase Matthew has used only once before, at Matthew 4:17, where it introduced His preaching of the kingdom. Here it introduces a second movement: the teaching of the cross. Everything before verse 21 gathers toward the confession, and everything after it moves toward Jerusalem.

The chapter divides into three beats that mirror one another. First comes a question about identity, verses 13 to 16, with the crowd's answers set against the disciples' answer. Then Jesus blesses Peter and describes what the confession makes possible, verses 17 to 20. Finally He announces His passion, Peter objects, and Jesus turns the objection into a lesson on discipleship, verses 21 to 28. Peter is the centre of all three, first as the voice of revelation, then as the rock, and then as the stumbling block. The same man is praised and rebuked within seven verses.

The two sayings of Jesus to Peter fit as a pair. 'Blessed are you', verse 17, is answered by 'Get behind Me, Satan', verse 23, and each rests on a statement about the source of Peter's words: from the Father in one case, from men in the other. The call to discipleship in verse 24 then picks up the very phrase of the rebuke: Peter is told to get 'behind' Jesus, and every follower is to come 'after' Him, using the same Greek preposition.

Verses 24 to 27 are tightly balanced, with a run of 'for' clauses that give reasons: lose your life to find it, because gaining the world means losing your soul, because the Son of Man will come and repay. The last verse, with its promise that some will see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom, leads straight into the transfiguration, which begins 'after six days' in Matthew 17:1.
context.historical:
Caesarea Philippi lay at the northern edge of Galilee, at the foot of Mount Hermon, near one of the sources of the Jordan. It was a largely Gentile city that Philip the tetrarch had rebuilt and named in honor of the emperor, adding his own name to distinguish it from the coastal Caesarea. The area had long been associated with the worship of Pan and other gods, and there was a cave and a cliff face of rock at the site. Some have suggested that the imagery of rock and the gates of Hades gains force from such a setting, though Matthew does not say so and the point should not be pressed.

The answers the disciples report show the range of expectation. People saw Jesus as John the Baptist risen, as Elijah whom Malachi had promised, as Jeremiah, or one of the prophets, verse 14. Each of these was high praise, and none was enough. Jewish hopes for the 'Christ', the anointed one, were varied, but were mostly of a king who would defeat Israel's enemies. Peter's confession would have been heard against that background, and it explains Jesus' command to keep silence, verse 20, since a political misreading was a real danger.

'Son of Man' was a phrase Jesus often used of Himself. It carried both ordinary and exalted meaning, since it could mean simply 'a man', and yet it also recalled the figure of Daniel 7:13 and 14 who receives an everlasting kingdom. Jesus says He must be killed, an idea foreign to the popular hope. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for rebels and slaves, a sight the disciples knew well, so the words 'take up his cross', verse 24, would be heard as a call to a shameful death, not as a figure of speech for minor hardship.

The 'binding and loosing' language belonged to the rabbis' vocabulary for forbidding and permitting, and for the authority to interpret the Law. The disciples would hear it as a grant of teaching and disciplinary authority.
context.canonical:
Peter's confession gathers several Old Testament titles. 'Christ' is the Greek form of the Hebrew mashiach, the anointed king of David's line. 'Son of God' echoes Psalm 2:7, where the anointed king is addressed as God's son, and 2 Samuel 7 where the promise to David's heir is framed as a father and son. 'The living God' sets the true God against the lifeless gods of the nations, as in Jeremiah 10:10, a point that would be sharp in a city given to Pan.

The rock has a long background. God Himself is called the Rock, Deuteronomy 32:4, and Isaiah 51:1 tells the faithful to look to the rock from which they were cut. Isaiah 28:16 promises a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation, and the New Testament takes this up of Christ, 1 Peter 2:4 to 6. Paul says that no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ, 1 Corinthians 3:11, and he also says the household of God is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus as the cornerstone, Ephesians 2:19 and 20. The image is therefore used with more than one reference, and Matthew 16:18 sits in the middle of them.

The keys recall Isaiah 22:20 to 22, where Eliakim receives the key of the house of David, so that what he opens no one can shut. Revelation 3:7 says Christ Himself holds that key. The authority to bind and loose returns in Matthew 18:18, given to the church, and in John 20:23, where the Spirit-given release of sins is described.

The call to the cross is echoed through the Gospels, from Matthew 10:38 and 39 to Paul's 'I have been crucified with Christ', Galatians 2:20. And Jesus' rebuke of Peter is picked up in Galatians 2:11, where Paul has to oppose Peter to his face, a reminder that the rock was a flawed man.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wants his readers to know two things at once: who Jesus is, and what kind of Messiah He must be. The first is given in Peter's words and in Jesus' blessing. The second is given in the passion prediction and the rebuke that follows. If the reader has only the first, the result is a triumphant picture of a king who never dies. If the reader has only the second, the death becomes a tragedy. Matthew sets the two in immediate succession, so that the confession is purified by the cross.

He also wants his readers to understand the church. The promise that Jesus will build His church, and that the gates of Hades will not prevail against it, is meant as encouragement to a community that knows persecution. The keys and the binding and loosing indicate that the church has real authority, given by Christ and exercised through those who hold to His word. Matthew is not writing a treatise on office; he is assuring struggling believers that they belong to something He is building.

Finally, the passage is a summons. Matthew makes verses 24 to 26 apply to every disciple, and the final promise of verse 28 turns the eyes of the reader forward to the vindication of the Son of Man. Those who hear the passage are meant to count the cost: whoever wants to save his life will lose it, and no gain in the world is worth the loss of the soul.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The scene records what was said and done at Caesarea Philippi. Peter's confession, Jesus' blessing and the rebuke are described, and they are not repeatable events. Nobody today receives a personal renaming or the same keys, and it would be a mistake to read Peter's words as the formula for a special authority belonging to one office through all time. What carries forward is the content of the confession and the pattern of the response.

The call to deny oneself and take up the cross is plainly prescriptive. It is addressed to 'anyone' who wants to come after Jesus, verse 24, and it has the force of a condition. Yet it must be read with care. It does not command the pursuit of suffering for its own sake, and it is not a general call to self-hatred. It is a call to give up the life one would hold on to apart from Christ, and to accept the costs that come from following Him.

The promise about the gates of Hades and the church is a statement about what Christ will do, and it is a ground for hope rather than for triumphalism. The warning to Peter that he can speak for God one moment and for men the next is a lesson for every believer, who should expect to be sometimes the vehicle of revelation and sometimes of error. We should never treat any one voice, however respected, as free from correction by Christ's own word.

debates.question: What is the rock on which Christ builds His church?

views.label: Peter himself
views.case: Jesus says 'you are Peter, and on this rock', addressing Peter directly and giving him the keys in the next verse. The Aramaic Jesus probably spoke would have used one word, kepha, for both name and rock, as John 1:42 shows in the name Cephas. Peter is the first to confess, and the early chapters of Acts show him leading the church, Acts 2:14 and 10:34. Roman Catholic tradition draws on this to speak of a continuing Petrine office, while many Protestants accept that Peter is the rock in a unique, foundational role without carrying on an office.

views.label: Peter's confession
views.case: The Greek uses petros for Peter and petra for the rock, and many take the wordplay to point away from the man to the truth he has just confessed, that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God. Many church fathers and the Reformers read it so. The church is built on the faith confessed, and so on the Lord confessed.

views.label: Christ Himself
views.case: Scripture elsewhere names Christ as the rock and the cornerstone, 1 Corinthians 3:11 and 1 Peter 2:4 to 6, and Augustine is often cited for reading the passage this way. Peter is the first stone, and Christ is the one who builds and the foundation under it all.

debates.bearing: The three are less far apart than they seem. Peter confesses, the confession names Christ, and Christ is the foundation. What the passage does not say is that Peter's authority passes to successors, and the dispute on that point turns on later tradition more than on this text.

debates.question: What is the power of the keys and of binding and loosing?

views.label: Authority to open the kingdom by the gospel
views.case: Keys open doors. Peter preaches at Pentecost and opens the kingdom to the Jews, Acts 2, and to the Gentiles, Acts 10. The binding and loosing is the apostolic declaration of what is forbidden and permitted according to Christ's word.

views.label: Authority of discipline and forgiveness
views.case: Matthew 18:18 gives the same language to the church in the context of discipline, and John 20:23 speaks of forgiving and retaining sins. Many see here the church's authority to declare forgiveness to the penitent and to exclude the unrepentant.

debates.bearing: The Greek verbs are probably best read as 'will have been bound' and 'will have been loosed' in heaven, which suggests that the church applies a decision already made there, and does not create the decision. Whichever view is held, the authority is derivative and bound to the gospel.

debates.question: What does it mean that some will see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom before they die?

views.label: The transfiguration
views.case: The very next scene, 'after six days', shows three of the disciples His glory on the mountain, Matthew 17:1 and 2. Peter later calls this the power and coming of our Lord, 2 Peter 1:16 to 18.

views.label: The resurrection and the spread of the church
views.case: After the resurrection, Jesus says all authority has been given to Him, Matthew 28:18, and some of the disciples would live to see the kingdom established in the world.

views.label: The fall of Jerusalem
views.case: Some take 'coming' as a coming in judgment within that generation, in line with Matthew 24. The destruction of the temple in AD 70 would be a vindication of the Son of Man.

views.label: The final return
views.case: Others believe the saying refers to the second coming and that 'some' sees it only in the sense that the kingdom's power begins to be revealed in their lifetime.

debates.bearing: The immediacy of the transfiguration and the way verse 28 is placed at the end of this chapter make the first view the most natural. The others may add depth, and none denies that the Son of Man will come in glory, verse 27.

study.originalLanguages:
The name play of verse 18 is in Greek petros and petra, a masculine and a feminine noun. The shift in gender is sometimes read as a deliberate distinction, but Jesus probably spoke Aramaic, in which one word, kepha, serves for both, and John 1:42 records the name as Cephas, which the evangelist translates as Peter. Greek needed a masculine form to give a man's name, and that alone can explain the difference. Whatever one makes of the debate, the pun is clear, and Peter is tied by name to the rock.

The word for 'church' is ekklesia, from the verb to call out. It is a common Greek word for an assembly, and the Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew qahal, the assembly of Israel gathered before the LORD. In the Gospels the word appears only here and in Matthew 18:17, so its use at this point signals a new gathered people, which Jesus calls 'My' church. He builds it, and it belongs to Him.

'The gates of Hades' uses the plural pylai, gates, and hades, the realm of the dead, standing in for the Hebrew Sheol. Isaiah 38:10 speaks of passing through the gates of Sheol, and Job 38:17 of the gates of death. The picture is of death's power as a fortified city, and the verb katischyo, 'prevail', means to be strong against or to overpower. The gates will not overpower the church, which implies that the church, built by Christ, is the one that advances.

The 'keys' are kleides, a plural for the means of access and authority. 'Bind' and 'loose' translate deo and lyo, and in Matthew 16:19 both are in a form that can be rendered 'will have been bound' and 'will have been loosed', a perfect participle with the future of 'to be'. That grammatical detail suggests that heaven's decision comes first.

In verse 22 Peter says 'Far be it from You', literally 'mercy to you', ileos soi, a phrase of wishing the thing away. He then 'rebukes' Jesus, epitimao, a verb Jesus Himself used when He rebuked the winds and the sea, Matthew 8:26. In verse 23 the phrase 'Get behind Me' is hypage opiso mou, and verse 24 uses opiso mou again for coming 'after' Him. 'Stumbling block' is skandalon, the trigger of a trap, and it describes someone who gets in the way of God's purpose. Jesus' diagnosis is that Peter does not 'think' the things of God, phroneo, a verb of mindset or outlook, not of mere opinion.

The verb for 'deny himself' in verse 24 is aparneomai, the verb Jesus uses in His warning to Peter that he will deny Him, Matthew 26:34. The one who now rebukes the cross will later deny the Lord, and the call to self-denial is the answer to both failures. The verb 'must' in verse 21 is dei, which Matthew uses for divine necessity, so that the cross is not an accident but part of God's plan.

typology.type: Eliakim and the key of the house of David, Isaiah 22:20 to 22
typology.fulfillment: God set Eliakim over the royal household, clothing him in robe and sash, and placing on his shoulder the key to the house of David so that what he opened no one could shut. Jesus gives Peter keys of the kingdom, and the language of opening and shutting returns. The correspondence is a steward given authority in the household of a greater king. The escalation is that the keys are the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and the One who finally holds them is Christ, Revelation 3:7. The type falls short because Peter's authority is delegated and derivative, while Christ holds the key of David in His own right.

God laid in Zion a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation, and the one who believes will never be shaken. The New Testament reads it of Christ, 1 Peter 2:6, and Matthew 16:18 shows the church being built on a rock. The correspondence is of a secure foundation that bears the weight of a community. The escalation is that the foundation is a person who is confessed and trusted, and the stones are living, 1 Peter 2:5. The type falls short only as a picture, for a stone cannot lay down its life, as Christ did.

The servant is despised, pierced and crushed, and bears the sin of many. When Jesus says He must suffer many things and be killed, verse 21, He takes this pattern as His own. The correspondence is the vindication that follows the suffering: He will be raised on the third day. The escalation is that this servant is also the Son of the living God, so that the suffering has infinite worth. The type falls short in that the Old Testament servant is not named, and the identification is given only in the light of Christ, Acts 8:32 to 35.

typology.type: The Son of Man receiving the kingdom, Daniel 7:13 and 14
typology.fulfillment: One like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives dominion, glory and an everlasting kingdom. Jesus says the Son of Man will come in His Father's glory, verse 27, and that some will see Him coming in His kingdom, verse 28. The correspondence is of a human figure given universal rule. The escalation is that He first suffers, a note not present in Daniel, and that the glory comes through the cross. The type is a vision and not a type in the strict sense, and so it falls short only in leaving the passion unspoken.

study.christ:
This passage is where Jesus' identity and His mission are set side by side. Peter's confession names Him the Christ, the Son of the living God. Jesus does not correct it: He blesses it and says it came from the Father. Each title carries weight. 'Christ' makes Him the anointed king of David's line, and 'Son of the living God' speaks of a relation to God that goes beyond a royal adoption. The same Gospel will show Him addressed in the same terms at His trial, Matthew 26:63, where the high priest asks whether He is the Christ, the Son of God. At His trial He answers with the Son of Man of Daniel 7, joining the two strands.

Then, within moments, comes the shock: this Christ must suffer, be killed and be raised. The word 'must' makes the cross a matter of divine purpose. Jesus does not drift into death; He sets His face toward it from this point on. Peter's protest shows how natural it is to want a Christ without a cross, and Jesus' sharp reply shows that such a Christ is no Christ at all. The temptation that Jesus faced in the wilderness, a kingdom without suffering, comes again through the lips of a friend, Matthew 4:8 to 10.

The passage also shows Him as the builder of the church. 'I will build My church' is a claim that only God could make, since He alone could promise that the gates of Hades would not prevail. It is the risen Lord who will see this through, and so the promise carries the shadow of the empty tomb. The one who stands against the gates of death is the one who will pass through them and break them.

And He is the pattern of the discipleship He asks. 'Whoever loses his life for My sake will find it', verse 25, is what He will do first. The cross He tells others to take up is His own, and He goes before them. Paul says the same: He loved me and gave Himself for me, Galatians 2:20. The final verses place Him as the judge who will repay each according to his deeds, verse 27, echoing Psalm 62:12 and bringing the Lord of the church to the end of the story.

A caution is needed about the rock. To say that Christ builds on Peter's confession is not to make Peter a second foundation alongside Christ. Paul says no one can lay another foundation than the one already laid, 1 Corinthians 3:11, and the church's security is finally in the Builder and not in any of the stones.
study.god:
The first thing the passage teaches about God is that He reveals. Jesus says that flesh and blood did not reveal this to Peter, but 'My Father in heaven', verse 17. Knowing who Jesus is cannot be reached by intelligence or experience alone, and it is a gift. This stands against every attempt to produce faith by cleverness or pressure, and it grounds the confidence of every believer: if they know the Son, it is because the Father has shown Him to them.

Second, the passage shows God as the one who builds and who protects what He builds. 'I will build My church' is a promise in the first person singular, and the gates of Hades will not prevail. The power of death is real, and Scripture does not play it down, yet it is a power that has an edge and a limit. This is the doctrine of divine preservation in a form that a persecuted community could hold: the church is not held up by its own strength, and it cannot be torn down by its enemies.

Third, God's ways are not man's ways. Peter's objection is the objection of a man who thinks the way people think, and Jesus says so: you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men. God's wisdom takes the road of suffering, and His victory comes through a death. This is a tension that the whole Bible holds, between the sovereignty that no force can overthrow and the choice to win through weakness. It is resolved in the cross, as Paul says, where God's weakness is stronger than men, 1 Corinthians 1:25.

Fourth, God is the judge who will repay each person according to what he has done, verse 27. This is a sober note after the call to follow, and it gives the call its seriousness. The one who gives His glory to the Son also gives Him the task of judging.

For worship, the passage gives us a pattern. We confess with Peter, we receive the knowledge as a gift, and we bow to the way of the cross. A worship that celebrates the glory of Christ but leaves out His suffering is not the worship of this passage, and a worship that dwells on the suffering and forgets the glory is equally incomplete. The Father who revealed His Son is to be praised for both.

crossReferences.note: The key of the house of David is placed on Eliakim's shoulder, so that what he opens no one can shut. It supplies the background for the keys of the kingdom, and shows that the language is one of stewardship in the household of a greater king, not of ownership.

The risen Christ describes Himself as the one who holds the key of David, who opens and no one shuts. It makes clear that the keys given to Peter are a share in an authority that remains Christ's own.

The same language of binding and loosing is given to the church in the setting of discipline and agreement in prayer. It shows that the authority in Matthew 16:19 is not confined to one man, though Peter receives it first.

After the resurrection Jesus breathes on the disciples and speaks of forgiving and retaining sins. It is a second account of the same authority, linked here to the gift of the Spirit and to the proclamation of the gospel.

Paul says no one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ. It guards the reading of the rock, since whatever role Peter has, the foundation of the church is Christ Himself.

The household of God is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets with Christ Jesus as cornerstone. It shows the apostles, Peter among them, as foundation in a derivative sense, bearing witness to the Lord who holds all together.

Peter himself describes Christ as the living stone and believers as living stones, citing Isaiah's cornerstone. The man named 'rock' points away from himself to the true stone, which is a telling comment on the passage.

God lays a tested stone, a precious cornerstone and sure foundation, and the one who believes will never be shaken. It is the promise behind the stone imagery of the New Testament, and it ties foundation to faith.

The Son of Man receives from the Ancient of Days dominion and an everlasting kingdom. It is the background for Jesus' favorite title and for the promise that the Son of Man will come in glory, verse 27.

The temptation to have the kingdoms of the world without the cross, answered with 'Away from Me, Satan'. Jesus uses the same word of Peter in verse 23, showing that the same temptation now comes from a friend.

Peter's other great confession, in the same Gospel tradition: Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life, and we believe and know You are the Holy One of God. It shows the Peter of faith, and the pattern that confession is a grateful response to who Jesus is.

Peter later writes that he was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty on the holy mountain and heard the voice from heaven. It links verse 28 to the transfiguration and shows how the apostle remembered the coming of the kingdom in power.

Paul says he has been crucified with Christ and that the Son of God loved him and gave Himself for him. It is the apostolic echo of verses 24 and 25: to take up the cross is to share in what Christ has already done.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a human race meant to share God's rule and a serpent who offers a way to power that bypasses obedience. The temptation to take the kingdom without the cost runs through the whole story, in Adam, in Israel and in the wilderness testing of Jesus. This passage brings that pattern to a head in a friend's mouth: Peter says 'This shall never happen to You!' and Jesus says 'Get behind Me, Satan!'

The passage answers the question that the whole Old Testament leaves open: who is the one who is to come? The prophets spoke of a king, a servant, a Son of Man, and a stone. Peter sees that all of these belong to Jesus, and Jesus confirms that the Father gave him the insight. Yet the answer comes with a surprise that the Old Testament only hints at: the king is the servant, and the glory comes through suffering. Isaiah 53 and Daniel 7 are shown to be one story.

It sets up everything that follows. From verse 21 the road leads to Jerusalem: the transfiguration that confirms the glory, the teaching on the church, the entry into the city, the cross and the empty tomb. The church promised here is the church that will gather at Pentecost, spread to the Gentiles, and be called to take up its own cross. The keys opened the kingdom to Jews and then to Gentiles in Acts 2 and Acts 10.

The story ends with the Son of Man coming in His Father's glory with His angels, as verse 27 says. Revelation shows the gates of death overthrown, since Christ holds the keys of death and Hades, Revelation 1:18, and the church is a multitude that no one can count. What looked like the defeat of the Christ was the defeat of death, and what was asked of the disciples, to lose their lives for His sake, is repaid with a life that cannot be lost. In the new creation the foundation stones of the city bear the names of the apostles, Revelation 21:14, and the Lamb is its lamp.

quiz.q: How did Peter come to confess Jesus as the Christ?

options.text: It was revealed to him by the Father in heaven, not by flesh and blood.
options.note: Verse 17 grounds the confession in God's revelation, not human insight.

options.text: He reasoned it out from all the miracles he had seen.
options.note: The miracles pointed to it, but Jesus says the confession came by the Father's revelation, not mere reasoning.

options.text: He simply repeated what the crowds were saying about Jesus.
options.note: The crowds said prophet or Elijah; Peter's confession went beyond them by revelation.

options.text: He was told to say it by the other disciples.
options.note: The confession was Peter's own, given by the Father, not coached by the others.

quiz.q: How does Jesus redefine what it means to be the Christ?

options.text: The Christ must suffer, be killed, and on the third day rise again.
options.note: Verse 21 reveals a suffering and rising Messiah, overturning expectations.

options.text: The Christ will go to Jerusalem to establish His rule.
options.note: He does go to Jerusalem, but to suffer and die first, which this omits.

options.text: The Christ will avoid all suffering by God's protection.
options.note: This is Peter's error, which Jesus sharply rebukes.

options.text: The Christ will conquer Rome by military force.
options.note: Jesus rejects a political-military messiahship; His victory comes through the cross.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus rebuke Peter so sharply after praising him?

options.text: Peter opposed the cross, setting his mind on human things rather than God's.
options.note: Verse 23 names Peter a stumbling block for minding the things of men.

options.text: Peter spoke without waiting to be asked.
options.note: The problem was not his boldness but the substance, resisting God's plan of the cross.

options.text: Peter doubted that Jesus was the Christ.
options.note: Peter had just confessed Him; his error was about the way of the Christ, not His identity.

options.text: Peter wanted Jesus to suffer more than necessary.
options.note: The opposite; Peter wanted to spare Jesus the cross altogether.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say it costs to follow Him?

options.text: Self-denial, taking up one's cross, and losing one's life for His sake to find it.
options.note: Verses 24-25 lay out the way of the cross for every follower.

options.text: A willingness to give up some comforts for His cause.
options.note: It involves sacrifice, but Jesus asks for the whole self, not just some comforts.

options.text: Gaining as much of the world as possible for the kingdom.
options.note: Jesus warns that gaining the world at the cost of the soul is ruin, the reverse of this.

options.text: Nothing at all; following Jesus is without cost.
options.note: Jesus explicitly names the cost as cross-bearing and self-denial.

quiz.q: What is promised about the church Jesus builds?

options.text: Jesus Himself builds it on the confession of Christ, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
options.note: Verse 18 promises an indestructible church built by Christ.

options.text: The church will be strong as long as its leaders are faithful.
options.note: Leaders matter, but the promise rests on Christ the builder, not on human faithfulness.

options.text: The church will never face any opposition or death.
options.note: Death and opposition come, but cannot overpower it; this overstates the promise.

options.text: The church depends entirely on Peter's personal authority.
options.note: It is Christ's church, built by Him; the promise magnifies the builder, not Peter alone.

questions: Jesus asks everyone the same question: who do you say I am? How would your honest daily life answer that question this week?
Peter confessed rightly yet resisted the cross. Where are you tempted to want a Christ of glory without the way of the cross?
Jesus says whoever loses his life for His sake will find it. What would it look like to lose your life for Him in one concrete area right now?
The whole world is not worth the soul. Where are you tempted to trade something eternal for something passing?
True confession of Christ is a gift of the Father. How does that move you from pride in your faith to gratitude and prayer for others?

translationNotes.note: There is a wordplay in Greek between Petros, Peter, meaning a stone, and petra, meaning bedrock; the church is built on the rock, whether understood as Peter the confessor or the confession of Christ, and in either case by Christ the builder.
The gates of Hades pictures the power and realm of death; the promise is that death itself cannot overpower the church Christ builds.
Binding and loosing was rabbinic language for declaring what is forbidden or permitted, and for the authority to include or exclude; the same authority is given to the wider church in Matthew 18:18.
